extracted.intended_audience: media scholars, journalism students, and practicing journalists
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and summarizing the criteria and forces that determine what gets covered in local news (what makes a story ‘newsworthy’ at the city/neighborhood level). Useful for media researchers, newsroom strategists, or journalists seeking to understand coverage selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic Motives of Media Owners
rubrics_metrics.description: Owners and managers prioritize cost-efficiency, audience size within the target geography, suburban audience priorities, and advertiser preferences when deciding coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains why ownership-level incentives push newsrooms toward stories that maximize audience and minimize cost. Includes subfactors: cost-efficiency (cheap-to-produce stories), audience size in target geography (stories that attract local readers/viewers), suburban audience priorities (coverage oriented to rings around the city, not only the urban core), and advertiser preferences (content that doesn't alienate advertisers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional Motives of Journalists
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists' career incentives and newsroom practices — including desire for career advancement, reliance on official sources, beat structure, and daily deadline pressures — shape story selection and framing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highlights how reporters’ professional goals and routines bias coverage toward official sources and easily routinized beats. Guidance includes: career advancement/making a name (stories that build reputation), reliance on official sources (police, courts, mayor), beat structure (news organized by institutional beats), and daily deadline pressures (favoring quick, routinized reporting over slow investigations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategies of Media-Wise Politicians
rubrics_metrics.description: Politicians use stagecraft, pseudo-events, spin, and cultivated source-reporter relationships to shape what becomes local news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes how political actors manufacture or stage events (press conferences, photo ops) to attract coverage; use pseudo-events timed for cameras; run spin operations; and build relationships with reporters to increase coverage likelihood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crime and accidents
rubrics_metrics.description: Crimes and accidents are more likely to be covered because they are easy to cover, dramatic, and have official sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly listed as a primary implicit criterion: such events provide official sources (police, courts), clear dramatic elements, and straightforward, fast reporting fits newsroom routines — which explains disproportionate coverage relative to policy issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local geography (neighborhood identification)
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories tied to neighborhoods or local places that readers identify with are privileged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coverage favors items that map onto recognizable neighborhoods or local geographies; this helps audience connection and retention. Geographic fit can trump abstract or citywide policy stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local elites
rubrics_metrics.description: Coverage concentrates on local elites — mayor, council, police chief — as primary news actors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists' reliance on official sources and institutions means stories involving recognized local elites receive priority, shaping which issues appear on the agenda.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visual potential
rubrics_metrics.description: Events with strong visual elements (fires, crashes) are favored, particularly by television and photo-driven outlets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stories that produce compelling images or video are more likely to be assigned and promoted because visuals attract audiences and are easier to package for broadcast or online platforms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pseudo-events scheduled for media
rubrics_metrics.description: Media-targeted events staged by actors specifically to generate coverage (press conferences, photo ops) effectively create news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because such events are timed and designed for reporters, they fit newsroom routines and source relationships, increasing their chances of coverage compared with unscripted policy developments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sports (local teams)
rubrics_metrics.description: Local sports coverage is a durable source of community interest and receives consistent attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sports provide regular, high-engagement content linked to local identity; newsrooms allocate resources to cover games and team-related developments even when other issues may be more consequential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weather
rubrics_metrics.description: Weather events are routinely covered due to immediate relevance and broad audience interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weather reporting is inexpensive, recurrent, and of immediate practical use, making it a consistent component of local news schedules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fitting suburban audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories are selected to draw readers from suburban rings around the city, not exclusively the urban core.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newsrooms tailor coverage to the demographic and geographic composition of their audience; suburban priorities can shape what is reported and how city issues are framed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding deep policy/urban issues lacking drama
rubrics_metrics.description: In-depth policy, development, and urban-issues coverage that lacks dramatic or visual elements tends to be under-covered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because such stories are often complex, time-consuming to report, and less immediately engaging, they receive less newsroom attention despite large public impact (e.g., housing, transit, education).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pack journalism / story already picked up by other local outlets
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories that have been picked up across local outlets are more likely to be further covered (pack journalism effect).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Once multiple outlets cover a story, it gains momentum and becomes self-reinforcing; this can amplify certain events and suppress diversity of topics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coverage choices have urban policy consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Selective coverage patterns (favoring crime, visuals, pseudo-events) lead to under-coverage of critical public policy areas, depressing public engagement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key insight from Kaniss: news selection is not neutral — patterns of what local media cover shape public awareness, civic engagement, and ultimately policy outcomes by privileging some issues and marginalizing others.
